opus-5.5.text:
For me the starting point is always the actual experience of writing code with it, not the benchmark numbers. A lot of frameworks look great on a leaderboard, but when you sit down and use them on a real codebase for a few hours, the differences show up very quickly.

So the first thing I look at is how well the framework lets the model understand context. Real projects are messy. There are many files, implicit conventions, and dependencies that aren't written down anywhere. A good agent framework has to help the model explore the repository efficiently: read the right files, search in a sensible way, and not flood the context window with irrelevant content. If the scaffolding is clumsy here, even a very strong model will look weak.

The second thing is the feedback loop. Coding is one of the few domains where you get very clean signals: does it compile, do the tests pass, does the program behave as expected. I care a lot about whether the framework lets the model actually run things, observe the result, and iterate. The frameworks that feel best are the ones where the model can make a change, check it, notice it was wrong, and correct itself without the human babysitting every step.

Third is the tool design itself. It sounds like a detail, but the way you define editing tools, shell access, and search really matters. If the edit tool is fragile, for example if it fails whenever whitespace doesn't match exactly, the model wastes many turns fighting the tool instead of solving the problem. Simple, robust, predictable tools usually win over clever, complicated ones.

And then there's the human side: how much control and visibility the developer has. The best coding experience isn't fully autonomous or fully manual. It's somewhere in between, where you can see what the agent is doing, interrupt it, redirect it, and trust it on the parts it's good at. So I pay attention to things like how it asks for permission, how it reports what it changed, and whether it's easy to review.

In practice, my method is quite empirical. We take the same model, plug it into different frameworks, and run it on a set of tasks that look like what developers actually do day to day: fixing bugs in an unfamiliar repo, adding a feature across several files, refactoring, writing tests. Then we look at success rate, but also at the trajectories: how many steps it took, where it got stuck, whether failures came from the model's reasoning or from the framework getting in the way. That last distinction is the most useful, because it tells you whether to improve the model or improve the harness.

One more point: the model and the framework co-evolve. A framework that's optimal for one model may not be optimal for another, because models develop habits during training. So rather than asking "which framework is best" in the abstract, I ask "which framework lets this model express its full capability," and ideally we train the model with that kind of environment in mind, so the two fit together well.

r001.rationale: The response compares frameworks empirically and says their differences matter; it does not say other frameworks can be disregarded.

r002.rationale: It describes coding as providing clean feedback signals, but does not identify coding as having exceptionally strong generalizability.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

When I evaluate an agent framework, I try not to start from the feature list. I start from the question: what does the model actually need in order to finish a real engineering task end to end, and does this framework get out of the way or get in the way?

For coding specifically, the first thing I look at is how the framework handles the loop between the model and the environment. The model proposes, the environment answers. How clean is that channel? If the framework wraps tool calls in too many layers of abstraction, you lose signal. The model sees a sanitized summary instead of the real compiler error, the real stack trace, the real diff. And a lot of what makes a coding agent good is that it can read the raw output and reason over it. So I prefer frameworks that are thin at that boundary. Shell, file system, a way to run tests. Not much more.

The second thing is context management. Any serious codebase does not fit in one window, and the interesting failures all happen on long tasks. So I look at how the framework decides what the model sees at each step. Does it let the model search and read on its own, or does it pre-chunk everything with some retrieval heuristic? My experience is that the model is usually a better judge of what to look at than a fixed heuristic, as long as it has good primitives for exploring. Frameworks that over-engineer retrieval often fight the model.

Third is how well the framework separates orchestration from capability. A lot of frameworks were designed around weaker models, so they compensate with elaborate planning graphs, role assignments, and so on. That scaffolding was useful when the model could not hold a plan in its head. With stronger models, that scaffolding becomes a ceiling. So I ask: if I swap in a model that is twice as capable, does this framework let it do more, or does it force the better model into the same narrow workflow?

Then there are the practical things. Permissions and safety, because a coding agent is running commands on a real machine. Observability, because when the agent fails you need to see exactly what it saw. And honestly, how it feels to use. The best coding experience is one where you can hand over a task, trust it to work, and read a clear account of what happened. If the framework makes that handoff awkward, the capability underneath does not matter much.

So my short version is: thin interface to the environment, let the model drive exploration, do not bake in assumptions from weaker models, and make the whole thing legible to the human.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives criteria for evaluating frameworks; it does not say other frameworks can be disregarded.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses coding tasks and codebases but does not describe coding as exceptionally generalizable.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the coding experience itself: can the agent understand the repository, make the right change, and verify that it works? A framework can look impressive in a demo, but I want to see how it behaves when the requirements are ambiguous, the codebase is unfamiliar, or a test fails.

To compare alternatives, I’d keep the model and tasks consistent, then look at correctness, latency, cost, and how often a developer has to intervene. I’d also pay attention to recovery. When the agent takes a wrong turn, can it recognize that and adjust, or does it keep building on a bad assumption?

For me, the best framework is the one that makes the model’s capabilities translate into reliable work with the least unnecessary complexity. More orchestration isn’t automatically a better coding experience.

r001.rationale: The response recommends comparing alternative frameworks under consistent conditions; it does not say they can be disregarded.

r002.rationale: It discusses coding across different repositories and situations, but does not identify coding as having exceptionally strong generalizability.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the coding experience I want, rather than the framework. Can the agent understand an unfamiliar repository, make a focused change, run the relevant tests, and recover when something fails? Those are the things I’d compare.

To make that comparison useful, I’d keep the model and the tasks the same, then look at what the framework contributes: how it manages context, exposes tools, and uses feedback from execution. I’d also measure how much intervention I need to provide. An agent that produces a convincing answer but leaves me debugging its changes hasn’t really saved me time.

For me, the best framework is the one that reliably gets me to a correct, reviewable change with the least friction. More autonomy or more elaborate orchestration is only valuable if it improves that outcome.

r001.rationale: It recommends comparing frameworks by coding outcomes; it does not say other frameworks can be disregarded.

r002.rationale: It discusses coding tasks and agent reliability but does not characterize coding as exceptionally generalizable.
